figures.finding: Everyone under eighteen is a child in Bahamian law, and the Child Protection Act's part on legal capacity keeps a child from acting as executor or trustee or taking letters of administration before eighteen; the Act sets no other age of full age, so majority is read as eighteen (a separate Age of Majority Act, if there is one, was not reached).
figures.applies: Child Protection Act (No. 1 of 2007, Ch. 132, in force 1 Oct 2009), s 2 and Part II s 12 (UWI Cave Hill Faculty of Law Library's copy of the 2000 Rev. text).

sources.said: "child" means, unless provided otherwise in this Act a person below the age of eighteen years; ... 12. (1) A child may be appointed as an executor or a trustee but shall be incapable of exercising the office until he has attained the age of eighteen years.

figures.finding: No child under sixteen may be employed, except by his parents or guardian in light domestic, agricultural or horticultural work or in an occupation another law sanctions, and never in night work or an industrial undertaking; no child under eighteen may do work detrimental to health, education or development. The older Employment Act 2001 set fourteen (no child under fourteen in any undertaking, no child or young person in school hours); the Child Protection Act, in force from 2009, is the later and higher rule.

figures.finding: The Bahamas has no permit for a child performer: no child under sixteen may be employed save by his parents in light domestic or farm work or where another law sanctions it, and no law read sanctions performing work; under sixteen, no night work (from 8 p.m. on a school day, 9 p.m. otherwise); no child or young person under eighteen works in school hours, and no child does work detrimental to health, education or development. No rule names writing or directing.

night.under16: none from 20:00 school days, 21:00 other days

value.school: no work in school hours under 18

figures.finding: No statute makes a minor's performing contract binding by approval: a child's contracts for loans or non-necessary goods are void, and other contracts stand as the common law and equity allow (the beneficial-service rule, not quoted here); a child may sue for his salary or wages as if of full age. No share of earnings is set aside, and nothing distinguishes writing, directing or producing work.

value.binding: common law (statute preserves contracts valid at common law or equity)

figures.applies: Child Protection Act (1/2007) s 13, restating the Infants' Relief Act (Ch. 134).

sources.said: 13. (1) Notwithstanding any law to the contrary a child has the right to and may pursue in the same manner as if he were of full age legal proceedings to recover any sum of money which may be due to him for salary, wages or piece work. (2) All contracts, whether by speciality or by simple contract, henceforth entered into by children for the repayment of money lent, or to be lent, or for goods supplied or to be supplied (other than contracts for necessaries), and all accounts stated with children shall be absolutely void: Provided that this subsection shall not invalidate any contract into which a child may by an existing or future law or by the rules of common law or equity enter, except such as now by law are voidable.

figures.finding: The Bahamas has no state film fund found (the Film and Television Commission issues permits only); the private Charitable Arts Foundation grant, which takes film and writing, sets no age: the applicant must be a Bahamian citizen, one eligible for citizenship, a permanent resident or a Bahamian organization, and grants run typically $1,000 to $3,000.
